goal: Hook at the class device station with three staged faults and the compelling question; a teacher think-aloud on one fault with the five troubleshooting steps, then pairs use the steps at the stations until each fault is found, fixed and checked.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes, after the hook): sort four pictured things as hardware or software, then sort small and large systems by input, process and output and point to where a fault could sit on the system-diagram (Candidate kept, zero days). Staged faults set by the teacher with the device settings and accessory cables only: volume off, mouse or headphone cable out, wrong window open, airplane mode. Paper path: picture fault cards that show what the device does after each chosen step. Pairs switch at the keys halfway. Device day, four ways: one device per pair, a few devices at stations with the other pairs on the paper version, one screen with a student at the device for each step, or no device. Safety: devices carried with two hands and cords behind the table; students never touch a power cord or a wall socket, never open a case and never change a setting the teacher did not stage; the last four minutes save or print work, shut lids and return devices. Base: Systems and searching lessons 1 and 2, as the retrieval sort. Credit (once): adapted from the Teach Computing Curriculum, archived 2023 edition, Year 5, Systems and searching. Provisional until the archived base is in the source store (later.csv L149).

goal: Two network-diagrams of one room, cabled and wireless, compared on distance, speed, convenience and safety; on invented situation cards pairs say which connection fits and why, and the class acts out a signal along a yarn line and through the air.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): trace a message on a given network-diagram, device to router to device. One card: a device finds an unknown open network in a public place; the sensible choice is to say no and ask an adult; a device joins only a trusted network. Neither connection is always faster or safer. Yarn held at waist height, walked, not run. Bridge (science grade 4 unit 3, weeks 11 to 14, comes later): the session needs no code or wave idea and stands on its own; science can later name this signal as one way information travels. Unplugged.

goal: A building with a front door and rooms: proving who you are at the door (a login on a pretend paper account) is sorted apart from what you may open (a permission, a key for one room); the words authentication and authorization come last, after the sort.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): three pretend-profile details, safe to share or not. Sensitivity: online safety and personal information; every login is a pretend paper one and no real password is said or written; no card asks what devices a child has at home; the teacher page carries health's "If a student tells you something" steps word for word. Unplugged.

goal: A device traced on a strip from material and energy in, through use, to waste out, with the benefit-risk-chart: how widely used devices affect resources and the environment, and one thing a user can do (use it longer, repair, recycle).
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): one benefit and one risk of a pictured system on the chart. Device-life strips carry a dated teacher source line (the federal environmental agency's electronics donation and recycling page, as of the day read). Sensitivity: no blame on families for how they dispose of devices; no one is asked what is at home. Opens the benefit-risk-chart unit 2 uses. Unplugged.

goal: End-of-unit assessment, about 30 minutes, unseen items: two new faults, one hardware (an accessory cable) and one software (a setting or the wrong window), each worked through the steps to a safe fix that is checked; a new room and two situations, which connection and why; six new login-or-permission cards sorted and one explained; a new device life traced with one effect on resources (material or energy in), one effect on the environment (waste out) and one user action.
note: Opens with settling and instructions, not a retrieval task (a check sitting's opener); the minutes go to the sitting. One prompt per code: E4-SYS-HW-12 by two faults, one hardware and one software, each found, fixed with a safe step and checked; the others by a written answer with its reason on new cases. Paper version and read-aloud for every item; the fault items run at a station or on picture fault cards (in a 30-minute period, on picture fault cards with no device close). Response time: day 6. Safety: devices carried with two hands and cords behind the table; students never touch a power cord or a wall socket, never open a case and never change a setting the teacher did not stage; the last four minutes save or print work, shut lids and return devices.

goal: Respond day: reteach by error letter from day 5, then each student answers the missed item again in a new form.
note: Opens with the most-missed wrong example from day 5 (APPROACH, How a day opens, b). Unplugged; a station for a fault reteach where needed.

goal: Hook: every pair follows the choose-your-path anchor story, then traces it: which numbered line is the event that starts it, which lines repeat, which line is the choice and where each answer goes; grade 3 step-cards become numbered written lines.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes, after the hook): follow a four-card step-card algorithm with an if and say where it ends. Sentence frame: "First the algorithm ___, then it ___". Words only: no flowchart or pseudocode (grade 5). Unplugged.

goal: Modify: the written number-pattern algorithm (start at 1, add 3, stop at 22) is rewritten with a repeat in place of the listed steps, then one line is changed to a choice (if the number is even, clap) and a partner follows it to check.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): order the five troubleshooting steps for a pictured fault, and say whether a wired or a wireless link suits the pictured room better (unit 1). Bridge (math grade 4 unit 7, weeks 20 to 22, comes later): students only follow the given rule with small numbers, which grade 3 skip counting already met; explaining the pattern's features stays math's. Unplugged.

goal: Make: each pair writes its own numbered algorithm for a game, a route or a story with an event, a repeat and a choice; another pair follows it word for word and marks the first line it could not follow; the writers fix it and hand it in.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): two new cards, login or permission (unit 1). The fixed algorithm is collected and read beside day 11; it is practice, not scored. Candidate kept, zero days: a reading-aloud partner step for students who write slowly. Practices CT8 and IC3. Unplugged.

goal: Two algorithms for one job (picking teams: captains in turn or count off by fours; sharing a limited supply: first come first served or an equal share) are laid out on step-cards and run on case cards of invented people with different needs; a benefit-risk-chart for each, and the class judges who each helps or disadvantages and why.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): first come first served or a time slot, who it suits, on one case card. Sensitivity: being chosen last and disability; the case cards are invented people, never classmates; teams are never picked in the room by skill in this session; the shared supply is never food; talk stays on the algorithm's outcome. Practices ESR1 and HCD10. Unplugged.

goal: Mid-year course-level check, standing as unit 2's end-of-unit assessment, about 30 minutes: each student writes a numbered algorithm with an event, a repeat and a choice for a new task and traces a new written algorithm to its end; judges two new algorithms for one job on new case cards; unit 1 sampled with a new picture fault card that shows the device's response after each chosen step and two new login-or-permission cards.
note: Week 11. Opens with settling and instructions, not a retrieval task (a check sitting's opener); the minutes go to the sitting. goal: Respond day for unit 2 and the check: reteach by error letter and gather fresh evidence on the missed items in a new form.
note: Week 12. Opens with the most-missed wrong example from day 11. Unplugged.

goal: Report: each student writes a short report in the table tool's report view beside the chart (the question, how the data was collected and entered, what the chart shows, one thing it cannot tell us); a partner writes one comment against three look-fors and the writer revises; chart and words save together or print.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): trace a numbered written algorithm with a choice to its end (unit 2); the report is a process told in steps. goal: Case cards of data collected about groups of people (a school survey of how students travel, a map of where people walk in a park, a store's count of shoppers by hour): who collects it, what and why, and which person and which group could be helped or hurt, set out on a data-table of the cases.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): which of two survey questions leaves someone out, and why, then which of two ways of sharing a supply leaves a group worse off (unit 2). Sensitivity: data about people; every case is invented for practice and no student is asked how they travel; plain words (helpful, harmful, unfair); no real student data. Weighing a collection as good or bad overall is left out. Unplugged. Base: Flat-file databases lesson 6. Credit (once): adapted from the Teach Computing Curriculum, archived 2023 edition, Year 5, Flat-file databases. Provisional until the archived base is in the source store (later.csv L149).

goal: End-of-unit assessment, about 30 minutes, pairs taking turns at the device: enter six new records into the table tool and sort a column; from a new small table make a chart and write three sentences beside it on the process and the result; a new case card: who collects, what and why, and one person and one group who could be helped or hurt.
note: Opens with settling and instructions, not a retrieval task (a check sitting's opener); the minutes go to the sitting. goal: Hook: the five-question class quiz runs, then runs broken after three questions were added at once; students predict, run and compare as they trace values through a counting loop and the quiz's score program in a trace-table, checking with the step-through.

goal: Build in small pieces: the anchor's broken build is rebuilt one question at a time with a test-table (what I tested, what I expected, what happened), so the bug is found in the last piece added; then a second buggy build, with bugs across the session in the order of steps, an event, a repeat and a choice, each found, fixed and tested again.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): the first wrong line in a traced program with an if. Kind: Understanding, not the frame's Fluency: the session modifies a working program, but the test-table and the piece-by-piece method are first taught today (For the lead 2). Driver and navigator switch at the halfway signal; a student who cannot use the keyboard or mouse navigates with the typed or list choice, never sits out. goal: Make: teams of three take the working quiz shell (its score logic already written and traced on day 19), plan their quiz on paper as numbered steps (each member's two questions, the right-answer choice and its messages, the end message), then build it, each member adding a part, testing it on the test-table and writing a short comment on what it does.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): what stops working if this block is removed? Students do not write the variable's start value, update or comparison (grade 5). Ten lines a part at most; questions are about class topics, never classmates. ELA lean: explaining a procedure is met in ELA grade 4 unit 2 (weeks 8 to 16); a school whose ELA runs late teaches the comment look-fors from a worked comment today. Driver and navigator switch at the halfway signal; a student who cannot use the keyboard or mouse navigates with the typed or list choice, never sits out. Provisional until the archived base is in the source store (later.csv L149).

goal: Feedback and revision: a reader from another team checks each comment against the code and writes one note; the team revises the code or the comment and runs every test again; the revised quiz is handed in.

End-of-unit, kept-work part: the revised quiz is scored on the rubric with a record for each member (three look-fors per member: the member's own working part; its comment checked against the code; the member's test-table rows, the part tested when it was added and again after the revision), built on day 22 and revised today before any score; it carries E4-PRO-PD-05 and E4-PRO-RD-07 into day 24, which stands for the rest of the unit's end-of-unit assessment. Candidate kept, zero days: the base's quiz-evaluating step is the reader's check. goal: Hook: a picture sorter calls every red shape a circle because every circle it was shown was red; students change one property of a training-set (all one color, too few examples, one kind missing, some wrong labels then corrected), predict how the output changes, then observe it with the class acting as the sorter.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes, after the hook): what changed when the sorter saw more examples? No faces, voices or named people in any set; no claim that a machine thinks. The one-screen sorter is tool work not yet built (the sorter trainer, later.csv L148), so the day runs on the paper path: the class as the sorter on picture cards meets E4-ALG-ML-02 in full; the teacher shows the one screen once it exists. Students do not train on a device (grade 5).

goal: How a child learns a new word (meaning, a few examples, asking why) set beside how a machine learns from many labeled examples with no understanding, on a two-column chart, with one written sentence of each kind.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): a training-set read as a table of labeled examples, a record and its attribute (unit 3), and one row of a trace-table for a three-line score program (unit 4). Unplugged.

goal: Biography cards of diverse people and communities in the history of computing go on the timeline with what each added: Annie Easley, Mary Golda Ross of the Cherokee Nation, Jerry Lawson and the women who first programmed one of the earliest electronic computers.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): place two tools on the timeline and say why one was made. Sensitivity: Native, Black and women's history; Mary Golda Ross told as her own work from her nation's and the agencies' own pages, never as a symbol; contributions, not barriers alone; no dates to memorize. Each card has a dated teacher source line (NASA's Easley biography; the US Mint 2019 Native American dollar page; the Computer History Museum), opened and dated by the unit writer; Easley's details are from memory, checked at source. Swap: a school may use people from its own community, each with a dated source. Unplugged. Sensitivity read before the case cards (docs/pipeline/briefs/sensitivity-read.md).

goal: A limit of an existing tool (a room-sized computer, a battery that runs out, a screen too small to share) and the new tool it led people to make, placed on the timeline and weighed on a benefit-risk-chart.
note: Retrieval (3 minutes): one benefit and one limit of a pictured system, and one resource it uses from material to waste (unit 1). No product or company names. Unplugged.

goal: Case cards of workers whose jobs changed when a new computing tool arrived (an office, a farm with soil sensors, a clinic with electronic records): what each worker had to learn and how they kept learning.
